steps.title: Mount a beurre blanc
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a classic beurre blanc in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Boil the white wine, white wine vinegar and chopped shallot until about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of syrupy liquid remains
If the house uses cream, add a spoonful now and reduce it by half
Turn the heat to its lowest, with the butter cold from the fridge in 2 cm cubes
Whisk in two or three cubes and let them soften into a creamy sauce
Add two more cubes as each lot turns creamy, lifting the pan whenever it feels hot
Season with salt, white pepper and a little lemon, and strain out the shallot or leave it in for a rustic sauce
Hold it warm, 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F), in a bain-marie or at the back of the stove
steps.distractor: Whisk two egg yolks into the reduction to bind the butter
steps.why: The reduction is boiled down hard first, with any cream reduced in it, and only then does the heat drop. Cold butter goes in a few cubes at a time so each lot emulsifies before the next. A beurre blanc takes no yolk: the butter's own milk proteins hold it.

steps.title: Clarify butter
steps.prompt: Put the stages of clarifying butter in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Cut unsalted butter into pieces
Melt it over low heat in a heavy pan, a bain-marie or a low oven
Let it bubble quietly without stirring while the water cooks off, skimming away the white foam of milk protein as it rises
When the bubbling slows and the fat looks clear, take it off the heat and let it stand
Ladle the golden fat off the top, leaving the milky layer behind
Strain it through muslin (cheesecloth) for a clean finish
Label and date it, and keep it liquid on the station with its own clean ladle
steps.distractor: Turn the heat up high and stir hard so the water boils off faster
steps.why: Low, quiet heat lets the water cook off and the solids part from the fat without browning; stirring would mix them back in. The foam is skimmed as it rises, the fat settles before it is ladled off, and muslin catches the last specks.

steps.title: Cook a fish à la meunière
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a fish à la meunière in order, from the raw fillet to the pass. One stage does not belong.
steps: Pat the fish dry with a cloth and season it with salt and white pepper
With the fish dried and seasoned, heat clarified butter in a heavy frying pan until it shimmers
Once the fat shimmers, dredge the fish in flour and shake off every bit of excess
Lay it in presentation side down and leave it until the edge turns golden
Turn it once, cook the second side and lift it onto a warm plate
Pour off the fat and wipe out the pan
Brown fresh whole butter to noisette, hazelnut brown and smelling of toasted nuts
Off the heat, add the lemon juice and chopped parsley
Pour the foaming butter over the fish and send it at once
steps.distractor: Brown the sauce butter around the fish while it finishes cooking, to save time
steps.why: The fish is dry and the fat shimmering before the flour goes on, so the coat fries crisp instead of turning to paste. The fish comes out and the pan is wiped before fresh butter browns, because scorched flour turns the sauce bitter; the lemon goes in off the heat.

steps.title: Make a mayonnaise by hand
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a mayonnaise whisked by hand in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Have the yolk and the oil at room temperature, and set the bowl on a damp cloth
Whisk the yolk with the mustard, a pinch of salt and a few drops of vinegar or lemon juice
Whisk in the oil a drop at a time until the sauce thickens and turns pale
Once it has taken, pour the oil in a thin, steady stream, whisking all the while
When it stiffens, loosen it with a few drops of water or lemon juice, then whisk in the rest of the oil
Finish with acid and salt to taste
Cover it and keep it cold, at 5°C (41°F) or below
steps.distractor: Chill the bowl and the oil well first, so the sauce sets thicker
steps.why: The emulsion must take before the oil speeds up: drops first, until it turns pale and thick, then a stream. Water runs out before the yolk does, so a stiff sauce is loosened before more oil goes in. Cold ingredients slow the emulsion, so everything starts at room temperature.

steps.title: Rescue a split hollandaise
steps.prompt: A hollandaise has split on the line. Put the stages of the rescue in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Take it off the heat and tell the chef at once
Look closely: a greasy split can be saved, but curds of cooked egg mean starting again
Put a teaspoon of warm water in a clean bowl, or whisk a fresh yolk with a spoonful of water over barely simmering water to a light ribbon
Whisk the broken sauce into it a few drops at a time
Once it takes and thickens, whisk in the rest in a thin stream
Check it coats a spoon and holds a line drawn through it, loosening it with warm water if needed
Hold it warm in a bain-marie, away from direct heat
steps.distractor: Turn up the heat and whisk hard until the sauce pulls back together
steps.why: The heat comes off first and the chef hears straight away. A greasy split comes back when it is rebuilt a droplet at a time on a fresh base, but a truly scrambled sauce does not: heat has cooked the yolk. Only once it takes does the stream speed up.

match.title: Butter from melted to black
match.prompt: Match each stage of butter in a hot pan, from melted to black, to what the cook sees and smells.
pairs: A quiet, pale yellow liquid with no browning yet
Loud crackling and a white foam as the water boils off
The crackling quietens and the first brown flecks appear
Hazelnut-brown specks and a smell of toasted nuts: stop it now
A deep, dark brown, past hazelnut but not yet black: the moment for vinegar and capers
Black specks and a bitter, smoky smell: pour it away

match.title: Emulsion faults and their rescue
match.prompt: Match each broken or failing emulsion to the rescue a cook reaches for.
pairs: Mayonnaise split into a thin, oily pool
Whisk it drop by drop into a fresh yolk in a clean bowl
Beurre blanc starting to oil out from heat
Off the heat, whisk in a cube or two of cold butter
Whisk it slowly into a spoonful of warm reduction or cream
Butter sauce set thick and dull from cold
Warm it very gently while whisking, never with a blast of heat
Sauce turned stiff and glassy, with a sheen of fat at the edge
Whisk in a spoonful of warm water at once
Whisk in a spoonful of cold water off the heat, then strain out the grains
Hollandaise scrambled into curds of cooked egg
Nothing brings it back: start a new batch
Whisk or shake it again just before use
